BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: Troughing moving onto the coast of British Columbia on Friday, paired with a building ridge over California, will shunt the majority of tropical moisture coming in on an atmospheric river to the north.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Breezy today. Near to slightly above normal temperatures through the week, rising to above normal by the weekend.
- Scattered showers near the Idaho/Nevada border today, and across the north on Thursday.
- Isolated to Scattered showers north Thursday with frontal passage. Then dry into early next week.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: High clouds will continue to increase through the afternoon, as a low moves eastward across northern Nevada (currently over northern California). While most of the area area will remain dry overnight, portions of southwestern Idaho near the Nevada border will get into the wrap around portion of the low, with isolated to scattered showers. Snow levels will be around 6-7kft MSL, although little if any accumulation is anticipated in regard to both liquid and frozen precipitation. Temperatures this afternoon will warm to be around 60 degrees in lower elevations, and 50s in the Oregon high desert and mountain valleys. Breezy west/southwest winds will also set in, strongest in the typical windy portions of the Snake River Plain with gusts to 20-30 mph. Gusts will taper off this evening with light winds overnight.

A brief period of ridging will bring clearing skies and lighter winds Wednesday, with high temperatures similar to that of today if not a degree or two warmer. This ridge will be short-lived, however as a short-wave and it's associated cold front will break it down and cross over our area Thursday. This will allow for slightly cooler temperatures (although seasonable for the time of year). While moisture looks to be rather limited with this front, it will serve as the focus for increased precipitation chances, 20-40% chance mainly in our northern zones, as it passes through from west to north. Precipitation chances will taper off quickly behind the front with northwest winds of 5-10 mph with gusts up to 20 mph in open terrain.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Troughing moving onto the coast of British Columbia on Friday, paired with a building ridge over California, will shunt the majority of tropical moisture coming in on an atmospheric river to the north. This flow will keep our area dry throughout much of the period. Periodic short-waves will work to break down the ridge beginning early next week, but with much of the moisture wrung out in the Cascades, the only tangible evidence would be increased mid-high cloud cover. Uncertainty in pattern evolution increases come Tuesday, although cluster analysis favors the pattern persisting.

BOU.name: Boulder / Denver
BOU.excerpt: A broad ridge aloft will expand over the Intermountain West Sunday through early next week. This will lead to an extended period of dry, mild, and pleasant conditions.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Precipitation will form across the mountains and foothills to the south of I-70 Wednesday afternoon through Wednesday night. Snow amounts will be between 2-7" with the highest values and worst road conditions in western Park County.
- Pleasant temperatures and dry conditions are expected Thursday through early next week.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Water vapor imagery shows relatively dry, zonal flow over Colorado between a departing trough over the Midwest and another trough over California. As a result, conditions will be dry today with breezy conditions across the plains.

The aforementioned California trough will move over Colorado Wednesday afternoon. This is a weak, compact system that will provide generally weak lift over a small portion of our forecast area. The main area that will likely (up to 80% chance) see precipitation with this system is the I-70 corridor mountains, southern foothills, and Palmer Divide. Despite the forcing being weak, there will be decent instability in the higher terrain especially in Park County considering the morning sunshine will create steep low level lapse rates. Showers and potentially a couple of thunderstorms will develop in the afternoon in this area. By the evening, the showers will turn into more stratiform precipitation and will spread out slightly. Model guidance is starting to spread out a bit for this system as a few higher end solutions have recently come in. Those seemingly indicate the potential this system could have to produce impactful snow especially along Highway 285 in Park County and some areas in the far southwestern foothills. The forecast currently calls for roughly 2-7" of snow mainly in Park County and adjacent areas above 7,500 feet. If there is an increasing trend in the precipitation amounts for this system, a Winter Weather Advisory may be needed due to poor travel conditions Wednesday night. However, there is uncertainty with the exact track of this system and if it were to go farther south, rain and snow amounts could be much lower. If the system tracks farther north, precipitation could expand further northward in the mountains but the precipitation across the plains will still be very limited.
On Thursday, a ridge aloft will move over Colorado which will dry conditions out. It will stay relatively cool with highs in the 50s across the plains.

A very weak shortwave trough will move just to the north of Colorado late Friday into Saturday. There is very limited moisture with this system and only a slight chance (20%) that any precipitation occurs in the mountains.
A broad ridge aloft will expand over the Intermountain West Sunday through early next week. This will lead to an extended period of dry, mild, and pleasant conditions.

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: Monday-Tuesday...Dry westerly flow aloft will continue with a progressive pattern of fast moving shortwave troughs aloft moving across our forecast area, but producing no precipitation due to relatively dry low and mid levels.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Near average temperatures and mostly dry conditions are expected through the rest of the work week.
- Warmer temperatures are expected to return this weekend with largely dry weather continuing.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: The short term forecast is predominantly controlled by an upper level ridge that followed the low pressure system that gave the region a mix of rain and snow. 700mb temperatures dropped on the backside of the low pressure system to about -2 degrees. This cold airmass will likely stay above us over the next couple of days as another low pressure system moves through the Southwestern Desert of the United States. This means for the next 48 hours the day time high's will be in the upper 40's to lower 50's east of the I-25 corridor and mid to low 40's for our higher elevation towns likely Laramie, Rawlins, and Saratoga. Overnight expect temperatures to drop to the mid 20's with a couple areas in Southeast Wyoming to hit around 30. In the Nebraska Panhandle it will be marginally warmer with temperatures ranging from 30 to 35F. As the short wave passes to our south tomorrow, it bring some cloud cover starting Wednesday afternoon. There is a very slight chance for precipitation to fall onto our mountain peaks but otherwise expect dry and cloudy conditions on the way home from work. The daily highs and overnight lows look to be relatively the same as today, although the cloud cover may keep us a tad warmer than what the models may have forecasted. The good thing about this ridge is the light winds across our area so the "wind chill" will just be the temperatures outside maybe minus one degree.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Thursday...Expect a decent warming trend as a well pronounced ridge aloft builds across the western High Plains states from the western Dakotas southward to eastern Colorado. 700 mb temperatures near 2 Celsius will yield maximum temperatures in the 50s.

Friday...A progressive shortwave trough aloft will move across eastern Montana and the western Dakotas, but only with some mid and high level clouds across our counties and limited lift producing no precipitation.
Saturday...The trough aloft moves into Nebraska and Kansas with a shortwave ridge aloft moving over Wyoming, continuing the dry weather for our forecast area.

Sunday...The flow aloft backs to westerly, inducing a decent surface lee trough across eastern Wyoming and eastern Colorado and producing a warming trend. 700 mb temperatures near 6 Celsius will yield high temperatures from the mid 50s to upper 60s.

Monday-Tuesday...Dry westerly flow aloft will continue with a progressive pattern of fast moving shortwave troughs aloft moving across our forecast area, but producing no precipitation due to relatively dry low and mid levels. Maximum temperatures will continue above normal, from the upper 50s to mid 60s.

GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: A dry forecast is favored for Thursday and beyond with warming above seasonal normals by the weekend. The only thing that could derail the dry forecast is the passage of another fast-moving low pressure system Friday PM.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Rivers and other waterways across southwest Colorado and southeast Utah remain high due to runoff. Several Flood Warnings remain in effect.
- A quick-hitting round of valley rain and mountain snow moves through along the I-70 corridor Wednesday afternoon through Wednesday night. Slick travel is expected to develop over mountain passes.
- Warmer and drier conditions highlight the remainder of the seven-day forecast.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: FLOODING CONTINUES ALONG RIVERS, CREEKS, STREAMS:

While today's forecast features dry conditions, flooding will continue along local rivers, creeks, streams, etc. as an abundance of water works through the system. Locations closer to the headwaters will see declining river levels with many sites falling below action stage today. Locations further downstream will see delayed impacts with some just cresting and others yet to crest over the next 24 hours. Visit water.noaa.gov for the latest river forecasts in your area.

A low pressure system currently located in northern California will track towards eastern Utah and western Colorado over the next 36 hours. This progressive system will bring valley rain and mountain snow to the region Wednesday afternoon through Wednesday night. Slick conditions are expected to develop over mountain passes with 3- 6" of snow possible above 10,000 feet. Lesser amounts are possible above 8,000 feet. Slow down and watch for rapidly changing road conditions if you are out and about!

The biggest point of concern and uncertainty with this system is how much convective enhancement will be realized on Wednesday afternoon. If rain/snow rates are enhanced from convection, the potential for impacts increases. Localized flash flooding is possible if stronger rain showers/storms develop over saturated or flood-prone areas, and hazardous travel conditions could develop over areas that see convective bursts of snow.

A dry forecast is favored for Thursday and beyond with warming above seasonal normals by the weekend. The only thing that could derail the dry forecast is the passage of another fast-moving low pressure system Friday PM. At this time, the more favorable moisture looks to remain north of the local forecast area, but we will continue to monitor this timeframe for some light valley rain/mountain snow.

PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: Sunday through Tuesday... After the weaker Fri/Sat system leaves our area, ridging develops and dominates through the rest of the period. Quiet, dry weather is expected across our CWA.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - A storm system will move across the area Wednesday into Thursday morning with high elevation snow and rain on the Plains.
- Overall, temperatures remain mild in the 50s to 60s for the lower elevations.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Currently...satellite imagery early this afternoon shows the upper storm system that impacted the region yesterday continuing to move eastward away from the area. Skies are clearing and dry conditions will prevail through the remainder of the afternoon. North winds continue to gust in excess of 30 mph out near the Kansas border. Winds will relax later this afternoon as the gradient eases. Temperatures this afternoon will top out in the 50s across the Plains and San Luis Valley.

Tonight...shortwave upper ridging will progress across Colorado overnight, with quiet weather and generally clear skies. Temperatures will fall into the 30s across much of the Plains while the San Luis Valley falls into the 20s by morning.

Wednesday and Wednesday night...a quick moving upper low is forecast to track east across Colorado during this period. A cold front will arrive on Wednesday afternoon, bringing northerly winds to the Plains. Model guidance is in good agreement with the timing and trajectory of the upper low. Expect showers to develop along the Continental Divide by tomorrow afternoon, and spread southeast into the Eastern Mountains and Plains by the evening hours. The primary focus will be across the Central Mountains, where favorable orographics will lead to a quick 3 to 6 inches by Thursday morning. Slick, snow covered roads and poor visibility are likely across the high passes of the Central Mountains. Across the Plains, showers are forecast to spread southward behind the cold front, banked along the Eastern Mountains, and south along the Raton Mesa overnight. Snow levels will remain high, mainly above 10 kft for the Sangre de Cristo and Wet Mountains, with 1 to 3 inches possible. High temperatures in the 50s ahead of the cold front, will fall into the 30s and 40s overnight on the Plains. That should keep precipitation liquid on the Plains, with the exception of the Palmer Divide where a few flakes are possible overnight.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Thursday through Saturday... As the Wed/Thurs system leaves our area on Thursday, a brief period of ridging will bring quiet, dry conditions on Thursday night and into Friday. A new system approaches the area Friday afternoon, with a positively tilted upper level trough in place over Colorado. This new system will be weaker than the previous one, considering its unfavorable structure and timing, leaving it with weak forcing and little moisture. Precipitation is expected to be very meager with this system. Should northwest flow strengthen, there is the possibility for snow accumulation over the Central Mountains. We will continue to monitor this system as it develops. By early Saturday, the system will be exiting our area. Expect breezy and dry weather through the weekend as the wave moves through. Near seasonal temps are forecast with highs in the 50s and 60s and overnight lows in the 20s and 30s.

Sunday through Tuesday... After the weaker Fri/Sat system leaves our area, ridging develops and dominates through the rest of the period. Quiet, dry weather is expected across our CWA. Seasonal to above seasonal temps are forecast as we get into early next week. Highs will be in the 50s and 60s, with some locations in the plains having the potential to get up to 70. Lows in the 20s and 30s, up to 40 in the eastern plains.

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: Following this storm system, this cooler, yet dry air mass will stick around through the work week as largely cyclonic flow dominates the western US.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Cool, dry, and stable conditions will persist across Utah and southwest Wyoming today and tonight.
- A weak system traverses the Great Basin on Wednesday bringing light valley rain and high elevation snowfall to northern and central Utah.
- Starting Thursday, quiet weather looks to persist as a strong ridge of high pressure builds across the western U.S.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Utah and southwest Wyoming remain between two troughs this morning on satellite imagery, resulting in largely quiescent conditions under a dry, stable air mass. Isolated areas of fog developed early this morning given calm and clear conditions, but is unlikely to return tonight given increasing mid-level clouds ahead of the trough to our west that will limit surface cooling.

As that trough continues to close off over the Great Basin, precipitation chances will increase first over the West Desert by early Wednesday morning, shifting over northern/central Utah by late morning. Low-level flow will become more northeasterly through the day, moreso favoring measurable precipitation over the Wasatch Back and areas east rather than the Wasatch Front. Still, precipitation amounts will be minimal, with the 75th percentile (25% chance of exceedance) showing around 0.25" of rainfall near Park City/Heber City. High temperatures tomorrow will be around 5-10 degrees below normal as this system brings cooler air into the region.

Following this storm system, this cooler, yet dry air mass will stick around through the work week as largely cyclonic flow dominates the western US. As skies clear later this week, we will need to monitor valley fog chances, particularly given above- normal soil moisture across the area. Over the weekend, a steady warming trend is expected as high pressure builds, with temperatures approaching 5-10 degrees above normal by Monday. Ensemble guidance suggests our next precipitation chances won't return until at least the middle of next week.

2660.travel_advice: Heightened avalanche conditions on specific terrain features. Evaluate snow and terrain carefully; identify features of concern.

product.author: Brian Lazar
bottom_line: On high-elevation alpine slopes, you can trigger an avalanche large enough to bury you.

The most dangerous slopes face northwest to northeast through east, where winds drifted snow onto lee slopes, forming thicker, more connected slabs. Below about 12,000 feet, avalanches will become smaller and more isolated.
You can find safer travel options at lower elevations and in wind-sheltered areas.

2755.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Spencer Logan
bottom_line: Most slopes lack enough snow to produce an avalanche. Steer around steep slopes near ridgelines with continuous, firm snow cover. You might find these slopes to avoid at high elevations.

2842.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

product.author: Kevin Studley
hazard_discussion: Avalanche Forecasting Operations Have Come to a Close for the 2026-26 Season
Have a safe spring in the mountains. Continue to remain vigilant and flexible while traveling in the mountains this spring.
OBSERVATIONS

Observations are still greatly appreciated. Spring-time observations are extremely helpful as forecast operations have come to a close. If you're out in the mountains, submit an observation to let the rest of the public know what's going on out there. Even a simple weather observation can be very useful.
• View recent observations HERE
• Submit an observation HERE
• Recent photos and videos HERE
Snow and Avalanche Information
• Dry Slab avalanche problems such as storm slab and wind slab avalanches are most likely during and immediately following a storm.

• Wet Loose avalanches are expected during warmups and (even brief) clear, sunny weather events, and rain events. Watch for pinwheels and rollerballs as an indicator the snow is becoming damp. If you're sinking into soft, mushy snow, it's time to turn around or find a different aspect.

• Wet Slab avalanches become likely during rain events and with multiple nights above freezing. Wet slabs occur when melt water pools and lubricates crusts or older persistent weak layers. Wet slab avalanches are notoriously difficult to predict.
• Cornices are large and often become unstable during prolonged warmups. Give yourself plenty of space above and below them. They tend to begin shedding during warming and/or rain events.
• Dry Loose Snow avalanches are expected during and immediately after a storm, particularly on shaded, north-facing slopes.

• Glide avalanches typically fail in similar spots year after year after an abundance of meltwater has saturated the ground or lower snowpack. Glide avalanches can occur in steep terrain, on smooth grassy slopes or on large slabs of rock. Look for glide cracks opening up during spring.
WEATHER
• Click HERE to view our Weather Station Map page with updated webcams
• Click HERE to view our Weather Tools page
• Spring weather patterns are often erratic and snow conditions can change quickly during spring weather. Be attentive to these changes and remain flexible with your travel plans.
• Rain on snow events can create dangerous avalanche conditions in a short period of time.
• Spring time means a higher sun angle, with direct solar radiation on the snowpack. Even a brief dose of sunshine can quickly alter the snow surface.

• Overcast skies and snow showers can open up to full sunshine in a matter of minutes. Convective snow showers can be spotty and difficult to forecast. Temperatures can vary depending on elevation and unexpected cloud cover can significantly alter a weather forecast.
OTHER CONSIDERATIONS
• Travel
• As people push into steeper, more consequential terrain, remember to maintain safe travel protocols and not let your guard down just because it's sunny and warm.
• During melt-freeze cycles, pay attention to "slide-for-life" circumstances, particularly during morning travel.
• Be mindful of terrain selection and timing. Identify terrain traps and be prepared to avoid/manage them.
• Spring Mindset

• Springtime is when mountain travelers push for bigger objectives. We have greater confidence in the stability of the snowpack and the high sun angle makes us feel ready to charge. As we start stepping out into bigger terrain in the mountains, be mindful of consequences (ask yourself, "If this slides, what will happen?"). Choose your terrain appropriately and manage new/surface snow problems accordingly. Be aware that dynamic weather can have quick impacts on the snow surface. A common theme I've noticed over the last 15 years playing in steep, snowy mountains is that experienced, seasoned people often get caught in small avalanches in big terrain during the spring. We have a tendency to underestimate "manageable" new snow problems like wind slab and loose snow. Pay attention to changing weather and know that small shifts in spring weather can have dramatic impacts on the upper snowpack.

2735.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Spencer Logan
bottom_line: Most slopes lack enough snow to produce an avalanche. You could trigger an avalanche on high-elevation north-, northeast-, and east-facing slopes, if you find firm, hollow snow, Just steer around these drifts of snow to avoid potential problems.
